rows.title: Carlos Alcaraz wins his 2nd U.S. Open at match delayed by Trump's attendance
rows.standfirst: The president's arrival delayed the match and left many ticketholders waiting in line. He watched from Rolex's luxury box.

rows.title: More than 90,000 Jeep Grand Cherokees recalled over potential loss of drive power
rows.standfirst: Vehicles impacted by the recall include 2022 to 2026 plug-in hybrid electric models of the Jeep Grand Cherokee.

rows.title: Postal traffic to U.S. drops over 80% after trade exemption rule ends, U.N. agency says
rows.standfirst: The de minimis rule that allowed small packages worth less than $800 to be exempt from tariffs ended on Aug. 29.

rows.title: South Korea charters plane to fly home over 300 workers detained by ICE at Georgia Hyundai plant
rows.standfirst: On Sunday, South Korean officials said they would send a plane to bring the detained workers home. Earlier, South Korea's Foreign Minister said his nation was "deeply concerned" by the arrests.

rows.title: Opinion: Susan Stamberg, trailblazer and NPR Founding Mother, retires
rows.standfirst: NPR Founding Mother Susan Stamberg is retiring. She became the first woman to anchor a nightly national news program in 1972, and helped loosen up the serious, stodgy sound of radio hosts.

rows.title: The U.S. government is taking a stake in Intel. It's rare — and it has some risks
rows.standfirst: In the past, the federal government has taken stakes in American companies during wars or economic crises. But now the government's motivation has more to do with the race for AI chips and technology.

rows.title: What happens to central banks under pressure?
rows.standfirst: President Donald Trump has been pressuring the Federal Reserve from a few angles. So we wanted to look at other examples of political pressure on central banks, to see what it might mean for us and for the economy.

rows.title: Under Trump, the Federal Trade Commission is abandoning its ban on noncompetes
rows.standfirst: Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson has called his agency's rule banning noncompetes unconstitutional. Still, he says protecting workers against noncompetes remains a priority.

rows.title: You can trust the jobs report, Labor Department workers urge public
rows.standfirst: A strongly-worded statement from Bureau of Labor Statistics workers comes a month after President Trump attacked the integrity of the jobs numbers they release monthly.

rows.title: Hundreds of South Koreans are among 475 detained in a Georgia immigration raid
rows.standfirst: "The business activities of our investors and the rights of our nationals must not be unjustly infringed," a foreign ministry spokesman said after about 300 South Koreans were detained.

rows.title: Why moms are leaving their paid jobs
rows.standfirst: Moms are quitting — or getting pushed out. Workforce participation for mothers in the U.S. has been dropping for most of this year, and the reasons are more complicated than return-to-office mandates. Today on the show, we talk to moms about why they left their jobs and to economist Misty Heggeness, who has studied the phenomenon. Find more of Misty’s research here. Related episodes:

rows.title: Cracks in the U.S. economy: Job growth slows 75% from a year ago
rows.standfirst: The U.S. job market showed more signs of weakness Friday, as the Labor Department reported just 22,000 jobs added in August. Revised figures show the economy lost jobs in June, for the first time since the pandemic winter of 2020.

rows.title: Have questions about homeownership or renting? NPR wants to know
rows.standfirst: Your input will help shape a new NPR series on renting, homeownership and everything that comes with it.

rows.title: Etsy sellers are being hit hard by tariffs and the end of the de minimis rule
rows.standfirst: For years, the U.S. was essentially "an extension of our domestic market," says an Etsy seller in Canada. But now the rules and costs are far more imposing.

rows.title: PBS cuts 15% of jobs in wake of federal funding cut
rows.standfirst: After Congress clawed back public media funding, PBS says it's cutting 15% of its staff, or more than 100 jobs.

rows.title: Trump administration launches trial program to fast-track electric air taxis
rows.standfirst: The FAA is seeking proposals for projects that will include piloted and unmanned operations with a focus on electric air taxis, also called an electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft.

rows.title: FAA seeks to fine Boeing $3.1 million for safety violations, door plug blowout
rows.standfirst: The FAA said it identified hundreds of quality system violations at Boeing's 737 factory in Renton, Wash., and Boeing subcontractor Spirit AeroSystems' 737 factory in Wichita, Kan.

rows.title: Fed's Cook claimed second residence as 'vacation home,' undercutting Trump fraud claims
rows.standfirst: Fed Gov. Lisa Cook referred to a condo she bought in 2021 as a "vacation home" in a loan estimate, which could undermine claims by the Trump administration that she committed mortgage fraud.

rows.title: What's costing you more lately, and how is it affecting you? NPR wants to hear
rows.standfirst: The NPR Network is working on a series about the rising cost of living. We want to hear from you: What costs are going up, and how are you coping? How is it changing the way you live?

rows.title: The U.S. now owns a big chunk of Intel. That’s a huge deal.
rows.standfirst: Last month, President Donald Trump announced an unusual deal. Intel, the biggest microchip maker in America, had agreed to give the United States a 10 percent stake in its business. That means the U.S. government is now Intel's largest shareholder — and a major American company is now a partially state-owned enterprise.

rows.title: Tipper Gore, Twisted Sister and the fight to put warning labels on music
rows.standfirst: 40 years ago, musicians faced off against a Washington committee over whether to warn parents about explicit lyrics.

rows.title: Health care costs are soaring. Blame insurers, drug companies — and your employer
rows.standfirst: Some 154 million people in the United States get health care through their employer — and for many, their costs are about to go way up.

rows.title: CBS shifts to appease the right under new owner
rows.standfirst: CBS' new owner, David Ellison, has taken concrete steps to address the concerns of the news division's sharpest critics — particularly President Trump and his allies.

rows.title: ICE raids, cooling on capitalism, and a Murdoch settlement
rows.standfirst: It’s … Indicators of the Week! Our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news. On today’s episode: the concept of capitalism is cooling in American minds; the U.S. policies behind the Hyundai ICE raid; and an influential family’s succession saga comes to a thrilling (and expensive!) conclusion. Related episodes:

rows.title: Are hotel rooms accessible for people who use wheelchairs? NPR wants to hear from you
rows.standfirst: Hotels have accessible rooms for wheelchair users. If you or someone you know has experienced problems with those rooms, we'd like to hear about it.

rows.title: Charlie Kirk's assassination sparks grief and rage online
rows.standfirst: Some conservative influencers mourned Kirk's loss, even as others quickly blamed the left.

rows.title: Home mortgage demand surges as rates drop to 6.35%
rows.standfirst: Rates saw the biggest one-week drop in a year, spurring a spike in new purchase and refinance applications.

rows.title: Inflation climbs in August as grocery and gas prices jump
rows.standfirst: Inflation accelerated in August as Americans paid more for gasoline and groceries. Over the last 12 months, consumer prices have risen 2.9%.

rows.title: NPR's next news chief built an international career at CNN
rows.standfirst: NPR has promoted Thomas Evans, its editorial review chief, to lead the newsroom through a period of change, following Congress' decision to end federal funding of public media.

rows.title: Hundreds of South Koreans arrested in a U.S. immigration raid are being sent home
rows.standfirst: U.S. immigration authorities are preparing to send more than 300 South Korean workers home on a chartered flight from Atlanta, a week after detaining them for allegedly working illegally.

rows.title: Trump's new $100K fee on H-1B visas will hurt the tech companies trying to woo him
rows.standfirst: More than half a million high-skilled U.S. workers are in the country through the H-1B program, which is heavily used by the big tech companies trying to curry favor with the president.

rows.title: Lawyers vs. engineers: Dan Wang sees U.S.-China dynamics in a new paradigm
rows.standfirst: In a new book, analyst Dan Wang uses "engineering state" vs. "lawyerly society" to explain how China got ahead and America stagnated.

rows.title: Defense Secretary Hegseth requires new 'pledge' for reporters at the Pentagon
rows.standfirst: The Pentagon is implementing new guidelines that will require journalists to sign a pledge and agree to report only approved and officially released information.

rows.title: In Gaza, money is falling apart
rows.standfirst: Israel has been blocking the flow of physical money into Gaza since the start of the war. So whatever paper cash was in Gaza before the war, that’s all that’s been circulating. It's falling apart from overuse.

rows.title: Trump adds $100,000 fee for high-skilled foreign workers in major visa overhaul
rows.standfirst: The president signed executive orders that would charge companies $100,000 a year to hire a worker on an H-1B visa and allow wealthy foreigners to get a visa for $1 million.

rows.title: 'We are all Jimmy Kimmel': What late night hosts are saying about Kimmel's suspension
rows.standfirst: The late night hosts warned about the future of free speech on their shows Thursday.

rows.title: Jimmy Kimmel's suspension shows power of FCC's Brendan Carr
rows.standfirst: In the eight months since becoming chair of the Federal Communications Commission, Brendan Carr has waged war against the free speech of those who have reported on, criticized, or satirized the president.

rows.title: Trump says talk with China's Xi yielded progress, including on TikTok
rows.standfirst: Officials have been working on a deal to bring popular video app TikTok under U.S. ownership to avoid shutting it down in the United States.

rows.title: Grocery prices have jumped up, and there's no relief in sight
rows.standfirst: Groceries saw their biggest jump in nearly three years last month, a worrisome sign for inflation-weary shoppers. Tariffs are contributing to higher prices for imported staples like bananas and coffee.

rows.title: The Fed cuts rates, America's FICO dips, and forever ends for sweepstakes winners
rows.standfirst: It’s … Indicators of the Week! Our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: Kimmel's suspension for Kirk comments sparks furor over free speech and censorship
rows.standfirst: After Jimmy Kimmel's show was suspended "indefinitely" for comments he made following Charlie Kirk's death, questions about free speech and just what is government censorship reach heightened levels.

rows.title: Democrats and Hollywood stars decry Kimmel's suspension as government censorship
rows.standfirst: High-profile politicians and performers are criticizing the suspension of Jimmy Kimmel's show as an attack on free speech. They are calling for the Trump administration and ABC to be held accountable.

rows.title: Kirk shooting videos spread online, even to viewers who didn't want to see them
rows.standfirst: Graphic videos of the Charlie Kirk shooting spread widely online, raising concerns over the emotional and political toll of exposure to violent imagery.

rows.title: ABC pulls Jimmy Kimmel off air after comments made about the Charlie Kirk killing
rows.standfirst: ABC announced Wednesday that Jimmy Kimmel Live! would be off the air indefinitely following comments regarding speculation swirling around the suspect in the killing of Charlie Kirk.

rows.title: Why beef prices are higher than ever (and shoppers are finally resisting)
rows.standfirst: American ranchers are raising the fewest cows in decades. Through the price increases, American shoppers have stayed loyal to their love of burgers and steaks — until now.

rows.title: Change is brewing in the coffee industry. What lies ahead?
rows.standfirst: Coffee growers are facing climate change, labor shortages and incomes below the poverty line. On International Coffee Day, we take stock of the industry behind the beverage.

rows.title: Spotify's Daniel Ek announces that he'll step aside as CEO
rows.standfirst: The founder of the world's biggest music streaming service says he'll remain at the company as Executive Chairman, and will be replaced by two co-CEOs.

rows.title: 'Like ice melting': Journalists warn press freedom is in decline across Asia
rows.standfirst: China's jailing of citizen journalist Zhang Zhan highlights a deeper press freedom crisis across Asia.

rows.title: Germany thrived in the first China Shock. But the next one could prove catastrophic.
rows.standfirst: The export-led industrial model that Germany has pursued for decades is now at a crossroads.

rows.title: Federal workers who took Trump's buyout are getting final paychecks and an uncertain future
rows.standfirst: Federal workers who took the Trump administration's buyout offer come off the payroll at the end of September. Now some are confronting fear, regret and uncertainty as they figure out what's next.

rows.title: EV sales surge in the U.S. ahead of Sept. 30 tax credit deadline
rows.standfirst: A $7,500 tax credit is available for the lease or purchase of many electric vehicles — but only if contracts are inked by midnight on Sept. 30. The result: The market for EVs is a little distorted.

rows.title: We're about to lose a lot of foreign STEM workers
rows.standfirst: Earlier this month, President Donald Trump announced a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitioners. Today on the show, we talk to an economist about how much H-1B visa holders have contributed to US growth, their effects on American-born workers, and why the United States’ competitors are taking advantage of this moment.

rows.title: Compass-Anywhere real estate merger could squeeze small brokerages
rows.standfirst: The deal, announced earlier this week, would combine the two largest U.S. residential brokerages by sales volume.

rows.title: What media consolidation means for free speech
rows.standfirst: Jimmy Kimmel’s brief departure from the airwaves triggered a wave of debate over free speech. Partly triggering his suspension was the government threatening to leverage its power over pending media deals. That’s in part due to a piece of decades-old legislation. Today on the show, we look at how the Telecommunications Act of 1996 set the stage for government meddling and corporate capitulation. Related episodes:

rows.title: Why friends are teaming up to buy homes
rows.standfirst: Buying a home is a conventional milestone for couples. But as home prices skyrocket, many Americans are buying homes with someone who isn't their romantic partner.

rows.title: NPR and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting clash as federal funding declines
rows.standfirst: NPR asked a federal judge to block CPB from awarding a $57.9 million grant to a new consortium of public media institutions to operate the satellite that connects the public radio system.

rows.title: Goodbye, Ari Shapiro
rows.standfirst: After 25 years at NPR and 10 years hosting All Things Considered and the last few years hosting Consider This, Ari Shapiro is moving on to his next adventure.

rows.title: How refrigeration took over the world
rows.standfirst: The next time you open your fridge, take a second to behold the miracles inside of it: Raspberries from California, butter from New Zealand, steak from Nebraska. None of that would have been remotely possible before the creation of the cold chain.

rows.title: Jimmy Kimmel reflects on his comic roots and how he broke into late night
rows.standfirst: The Jimmy Kimmel Live! host found himself at the center of a battle over free speech recently when his show was briefly suspended. He spoke to Fresh Air in 2013, when his show moved to late night.

rows.title: Argentina's bailout, a new way to cool data centers, and a cold holiday hiring season
rows.standfirst: It’s Indicators of the Week! It is that show where we parse the most fascinating financial numbers in the news and bring them to you.

frame: Up to15 visible Business-archive cards at four fixed weekly endpoints, restricted to each block; not a full-publication census
